findings.name: exotic-source
findings.title: the lockfile does not say where this version was resolved from

findings.explanation: package-lock.json does not say where npm:emoji-regex@8.0.0 was resolved from, so the entry cannot be read as a release from the npm registry. None of the registry's protections apply to it: the release cannot be yanked, advisories are not matched against it, and there is no publisher, provenance or download history to compare with the previous version. The version number the lockfile records is what the fetched manifest claimed, not a version anyone published. npm records neither a location nor a hash for a dependency bundled inside another package's archive, which is the usual reason for an entry with no stated origin; those bytes travel with the package that carries them and are covered by its hash. This is reported at info rather than at the level the policy sets for exotic-source, because that level is meant for a version fetched from a git repository or a URL, which is what a pull request can repoint under review, and not for an entry a monorepo or a bundling package manager writes for itself. An allow entry for exotic-source with a package glob takes it out of the report altogether.

findings.explanation: package-lock.json records no integrity hash for npm:istanbul-lib-hook@3.0.0. Nothing in the entry ties it to the bytes an install downloads. An npm entry with neither a location nor a hash is usually a bundled dependency, whose bytes travel inside the archive of the package that carries it and are covered by that package's hash; the lockfile does not say so, which is why this is reported rather than assumed.

findings.name: exotic-source
findings.title: the lockfile does not say where this version was resolved from
findings.explanation: package-lock.json does not say where npm:istanbul-lib-hook@3.0.0 was resolved from, so the entry cannot be read as a release from the npm registry. None of the registry's protections apply to it: the release cannot be yanked, advisories are not matched against it, and there is no publisher, provenance or download history to compare with the previous version. The version number the lockfile records is what the fetched manifest claimed, not a version anyone published. npm records neither a location nor a hash for a dependency bundled inside another package's archive, which is the usual reason for an entry with no stated origin; those bytes travel with the package that carries them and are covered by its hash. This is reported at info rather than at the level the policy sets for exotic-source, because that level is meant for a version fetched from a git repository or a URL, which is what a pull request can repoint under review, and not for an entry a monorepo or a bundling package manager writes for itself. An allow entry for exotic-source with a package glob takes it out of the report altogether.

findings.explanation: package-lock.json does not say where npm:mdast-util-to-markdown@2.1.2 was resolved from, so the entry cannot be read as a release from the npm registry. None of the registry's protections apply to it: the release cannot be yanked, advisories are not matched against it, and there is no publisher, provenance or download history to compare with the previous version. The version number the lockfile records is what the fetched manifest claimed, not a version anyone published. npm records neither a location nor a hash for a dependency bundled inside another package's archive, which is the usual reason for an entry with no stated origin; those bytes travel with the package that carries them and are covered by its hash. This is reported at info rather than at the level the policy sets for exotic-source, because that level is meant for a version fetched from a git repository or a URL, which is what a pull request can repoint under review, and not for an entry a monorepo or a bundling package manager writes for itself. An allow entry for exotic-source with a package glob takes it out of the report altogether.

findings.name: integrity-missing
findings.title: no integrity hash in the lockfile
findings.explanation: package-lock.json records no integrity hash for npm:nth-check@2.1.1. Nothing in the entry ties it to the bytes an install downloads. An npm entry with neither a location nor a hash is usually a bundled dependency, whose bytes travel inside the archive of the package that carries it and are covered by that package's hash; the lockfile does not say so, which is why this is reported rather than assumed.

findings.name: exotic-source
findings.title: the lockfile does not say where this version was resolved from
findings.explanation: package-lock.json does not say where npm:nth-check@2.1.1 was resolved from, so the entry cannot be read as a release from the npm registry. None of the registry's protections apply to it: the release cannot be yanked, advisories are not matched against it, and there is no publisher, provenance or download history to compare with the previous version. The version number the lockfile records is what the fetched manifest claimed, not a version anyone published. npm records neither a location nor a hash for a dependency bundled inside another package's archive, which is the usual reason for an entry with no stated origin; those bytes travel with the package that carries them and are covered by its hash. This is reported at info rather than at the level the policy sets for exotic-source, because that level is meant for a version fetched from a git repository or a URL, which is what a pull request can repoint under review, and not for an entry a monorepo or a bundling package manager writes for itself. An allow entry for exotic-source with a package glob takes it out of the report altogether.

findings.explanation: package-lock.json does not say where npm:once@1.4.0 was resolved from, so the entry cannot be read as a release from the npm registry. None of the registry's protections apply to it: the release cannot be yanked, advisories are not matched against it, and there is no publisher, provenance or download history to compare with the previous version. The version number the lockfile records is what the fetched manifest claimed, not a version anyone published. npm records neither a location nor a hash for a dependency bundled inside another package's archive, which is the usual reason for an entry with no stated origin; those bytes travel with the package that carries them and are covered by its hash. This is reported at info rather than at the level the policy sets for exotic-source, because that level is meant for a version fetched from a git repository or a URL, which is what a pull request can repoint under review, and not for an entry a monorepo or a bundling package manager writes for itself. An allow entry for exotic-source with a package glob takes it out of the report altogether.

findings.explanation: package-lock.json does not say where npm:space-separated-tokens@2.0.2 was resolved from, so the entry cannot be read as a release from the npm registry. None of the registry's protections apply to it: the release cannot be yanked, advisories are not matched against it, and there is no publisher, provenance or download history to compare with the previous version. The version number the lockfile records is what the fetched manifest claimed, not a version anyone published. npm records neither a location nor a hash for a dependency bundled inside another package's archive, which is the usual reason for an entry with no stated origin; those bytes travel with the package that carries them and are covered by its hash. This is reported at info rather than at the level the policy sets for exotic-source, because that level is meant for a version fetched from a git repository or a URL, which is what a pull request can repoint under review, and not for an entry a monorepo or a bundling package manager writes for itself. An allow entry for exotic-source with a package glob takes it out of the report altogether.

findings.explanation: package-lock.json records no integrity hash for npm:strip-bom@4.0.0. Nothing in the entry ties it to the bytes an install downloads. An npm entry with neither a location nor a hash is usually a bundled dependency, whose bytes travel inside the archive of the package that carries it and are covered by that package's hash; the lockfile does not say so, which is why this is reported rather than assumed.

findings.name: exotic-source
findings.title: the lockfile does not say where this version was resolved from
findings.explanation: package-lock.json does not say where npm:strip-bom@4.0.0 was resolved from, so the entry cannot be read as a release from the npm registry. None of the registry's protections apply to it: the release cannot be yanked, advisories are not matched against it, and there is no publisher, provenance or download history to compare with the previous version. The version number the lockfile records is what the fetched manifest claimed, not a version anyone published. npm records neither a location nor a hash for a dependency bundled inside another package's archive, which is the usual reason for an entry with no stated origin; those bytes travel with the package that carries them and are covered by its hash. This is reported at info rather than at the level the policy sets for exotic-source, because that level is meant for a version fetched from a git repository or a URL, which is what a pull request can repoint under review, and not for an entry a monorepo or a bundling package manager writes for itself. An allow entry for exotic-source with a package glob takes it out of the report altogether.

findings.name: integrity-missing
findings.title: no integrity hash in the lockfile
findings.explanation: package-lock.json records no integrity hash for npm:tap@16.3.10. Nothing in the entry ties it to the bytes an install downloads. An npm entry with neither a location nor a hash is usually a bundled dependency, whose bytes travel inside the archive of the package that carries it and are covered by that package's hash; the lockfile does not say so, which is why this is reported rather than assumed.

findings.name: exotic-source
findings.title: the lockfile does not say where this version was resolved from
findings.explanation: package-lock.json does not say where npm:tap@16.3.10 was resolved from, so the entry cannot be read as a release from the npm registry. None of the registry's protections apply to it: the release cannot be yanked, advisories are not matched against it, and there is no publisher, provenance or download history to compare with the previous version. The version number the lockfile records is what the fetched manifest claimed, not a version anyone published. npm records neither a location nor a hash for a dependency bundled inside another package's archive, which is the usual reason for an entry with no stated origin; those bytes travel with the package that carries them and are covered by its hash. This is reported at info rather than at the level the policy sets for exotic-source, because that level is meant for a version fetched from a git repository or a URL, which is what a pull request can repoint under review, and not for an entry a monorepo or a bundling package manager writes for itself. An allow entry for exotic-source with a package glob takes it out of the report altogether.

findings.name: integrity-missing
findings.title: no integrity hash in the lockfile
findings.explanation: package-lock.json records no integrity hash for npm:cliui@7.0.4. Nothing in the entry ties it to the bytes an install downloads. An npm entry with neither a location nor a hash is usually a bundled dependency, whose bytes travel inside the archive of the package that carries it and are covered by that package's hash; the lockfile does not say so, which is why this is reported rather than assumed.

findings.name: exotic-source
findings.title: the lockfile does not say where this version was resolved from
findings.explanation: package-lock.json does not say where npm:cliui@7.0.4 was resolved from, so the entry cannot be read as a release from the npm registry. None of the registry's protections apply to it: the release cannot be yanked, advisories are not matched against it, and there is no publisher, provenance or download history to compare with the previous version. The version number the lockfile records is what the fetched manifest claimed, not a version anyone published. npm records neither a location nor a hash for a dependency bundled inside another package's archive, which is the usual reason for an entry with no stated origin; those bytes travel with the package that carries them and are covered by its hash. This is reported at info rather than at the level the policy sets for exotic-source, because that level is meant for a version fetched from a git repository or a URL, which is what a pull request can repoint under review, and not for an entry a monorepo or a bundling package manager writes for itself. An allow entry for exotic-source with a package glob takes it out of the report altogether.

findings.name: exotic-source
findings.title: the lockfile does not say where this version was resolved from
findings.explanation: package-lock.json does not say where npm:test-exclude@6.0.0 was resolved from, so the entry cannot be read as a release from the npm registry. None of the registry's protections apply to it: the release cannot be yanked, advisories are not matched against it, and there is no publisher, provenance or download history to compare with the previous version. The version number the lockfile records is what the fetched manifest claimed, not a version anyone published. npm records neither a location nor a hash for a dependency bundled inside another package's archive, which is the usual reason for an entry with no stated origin; those bytes travel with the package that carries them and are covered by its hash. This is reported at info rather than at the level the policy sets for exotic-source, because that level is meant for a version fetched from a git repository or a URL, which is what a pull request can repoint under review, and not for an entry a monorepo or a bundling package manager writes for itself. findings.name: integrity-missing
findings.title: no integrity hash in the lockfile
findings.explanation: package-lock.json records no integrity hash for npm:typed-array-buffer@1.0.3. Nothing in the entry ties it to the bytes an install downloads. An npm entry with neither a location nor a hash is usually a bundled dependency, whose bytes travel inside the archive of the package that carries it and are covered by that package's hash; the lockfile does not say so, which is why this is reported rather than assumed.

findings.name: exotic-source
findings.title: the lockfile does not say where this version was resolved from
findings.explanation: package-lock.json does not say where npm:typed-array-buffer@1.0.3 was resolved from, so the entry cannot be read as a release from the npm registry. None of the registry's protections apply to it: the release cannot be yanked, advisories are not matched against it, and there is no publisher, provenance or download history to compare with the previous version. The version number the lockfile records is what the fetched manifest claimed, not a version anyone published. npm records neither a location nor a hash for a dependency bundled inside another package's archive, which is the usual reason for an entry with no stated origin; those bytes travel with the package that carries them and are covered by its hash. This is reported at info rather than at the level the policy sets for exotic-source, because that level is meant for a version fetched from a git repository or a URL, which is what a pull request can repoint under review, and not for an entry a monorepo or a bundling package manager writes for itself. An allow entry for exotic-source with a package glob takes it out of the report altogether.
